speech.text: Chipmaker unveils a laptop processor with all-day battery life.
Also ahead: robot vacuum learns to climb stairs.
And later, our number of the day.
This is Tech Bytes.
I'm Max Circuit, with Ada Volt.
A chipmaker has unveiled a new laptop processor it says can run for twenty hours on a single charge.
Independent reviewers have not yet tested the claim, Circuit Weekly reports.
And when does it reach actual people?
The first laptops using it will go on sale in the spring.
A home robotics company has shown a robot vacuum that can climb stairs using two small legs.
It will cost about one thousand five hundred dollars when it launches next year, according to Circuit Weekly.
Our number of the day: thirty percent.
A data centre powered by wind and geothermal energy has opened near Rake-yavik, Circuit Weekly reports.
Its owners say it uses thirty percent less energy for cooling than a typical site.
A startup has launched a satellite internet service designed for farms in remote areas, according to Circuit Weekly.
It says the service reaches speeds of one hundred megabits per second.
Seoul has started testing self-driving buses on two night routes.
The city says the buses will help night workers get home when other transport has stopped.
A safety driver stays on board during the trial, Circuit Weekly reports.
Thanks, Max.
Twenty delivery robots have started carrying parcels through two districts of Barcelona.
The trial will run for six months.
The robots travel at walking pace and stop for pedestrians.
Researchers at a battery firm say a new silicon design could let phones last a week between charges.
The company hopes to start production in twenty twenty-seven.
Still to come: medicine-carrying drones expand across Rwanda.
A new pair of earbuds can translate conversations in forty languages in real time, its maker says.
Travel should not stop at the language barrier, the company said.
Researchers have released an AI model small enough to run on an ordinary laptop.
They say it needs about eight gigabytes of memory and works without an internet connection.
A new handheld games console sold two million units in its first week, its maker says.
Shops in Tokyo reported long queues on launch day.
A recycling plant in Sweden says it can recover one kilogram of gold from forty thousand old phones.
The company wants to process two million phones a year.
Now, some quick bytes.
A Mars rover has photographed layered rocks in what scientists believe was an ancient lake bed, according to Starfield Journal.
Astronauts on the International Space Station have harvested tomatoes grown in a small greenhouse, Starfield Journal reports.
A rocket has launched a probe that will study the Sun's poles for the first time.
And finally: drones now deliver medicine to four hundred health centres across Rwanda, the operator says.
The average flight takes about thirty minutes, according to Circuit Weekly.
Health workers order supplies by text message.
Blood and vaccines make up most of the deliveries.
That is what patience buys you.
That's Tech Bytes.
From Ada Volt and from me, thanks for watching.
More news around the clock on Globit twenty-four.
This is News in sixty.
I'm Sam Night.
In Seville, temperatures reached forty-four degrees Celsius on Wednesday, the highest of the summer.
Doctors advise drinking water often and staying in the shade.
Some schools have moved lessons to the early morning, Bitport Herald reports.
Oil prices fell for a third day as traders expect weaker demand this winter.
Brent crude dropped two percent to seventy-one dollars a barrel, according to Ledger Line.
An offshore wind farm in the North Sea has started supplying electricity, Ledger Line reports.
The developer says its one hundred forty turbines can power about one point two million homes.
A research ship has mapped fifty thousand square kilometres of sea floor near Antarctica.
The maps reveal underwater canyons and an extinct volcano, according to Starfield Journal.
Biologists have described a new species of glowing mushroom found in the Atlantic forest of Brazil.
It emits a soft green light at night, Starfield Journal reports.
That's the minute.
Stay with us on Globit twenty-four.
Solar eclipse to be visible across northern Spain next August.
Also coming up: our number of the day.
Later: bees use the sun as a compass even on cloudy days.
This is Cosmos Desk.
I'm Doctor Nova Rayess, with Unit Eight.
A total solar eclipse will be visible across northern Spain next August, Starfield Journal reports.
Astronomers say the shadow will cross Bilbao and Valencia.
Hotels along the path of the shadow report that many rooms are already booked.
Northern Spain.
I will not forget it.
Unit Eight, our number of the day.
Our number of the day: about two.
A study of ninety European cities found that streets with many trees were about two degrees cooler in summer.
Researchers say parks also reduced heat-related illness.
A new study shows honeybees can find the position of the sun through clouds using polarised light.
The finding explains how they navigate in poor weather, according to Starfield Journal.
Thanks, Nova.
Storms have uncovered footprints left on a beach in Wales about seven thousand years ago.
